lec05kp06-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp06-p1-104.name: term:Cost function
lec05kp06-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp06-p1-104.text:
Cost function: add up how far the
prediction is from the target into one
number, the smaller the better. Here E =
½(t − o)².

lec05kp06-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp06-p1-105.name: term:Gradient descent
lec05kp06-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp06-p1-105.text:
Gradient descent: look at the slope of the
cost with respect to each weight and nudge
the weight in the direction that lowers the
cost.

lec05kp06-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp06-p1-107.text:
The weights of KP05 were given by rules;
this chapter lets the network learn them.

lec05kp06-u01-p2-bridge.text: A step has slope 0 everywhere and none at the jump, so gradient descent has nothing to use. Can we round the step so every point has a slope?

lec05kp06-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp06-p2-7.text:
Sigmoid: squeezes any number into 0 to 1;
larger a, closer to a step.

lec05kp06-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp06-p2-9.name: fig:lec05-kp06-p2#9
lec05kp06-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp06-p2-9.text:
Myth: the closer to a step the better.
In fact the larger a is, the narrower
and higher the slope peak and the
flatter both sides, so training by
gradient gets harder.

lec05kp06-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp06-p3-33.name: term:Forward pass
lec05kp06-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp06-p3-33.text:
Forward pass: compute from the input layer by layer; each unit forms
the weighted sum v, applies the sigmoid to get y = f(v), and stores the
values.

lec05kp06-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp06-p4-32.name: term:Chain rule
lec05kp06-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp06-p4-32.text:
Chain rule: when A affects B and B affects
C, the slope of C with respect to A is the
slope of C with respect to B times the slope
of B with respect to A.

lec05kp06-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp06-p4-33.text: $\frac{\partial E}{\partial w}=\frac{\partial E}{\partial o}\cdot\frac{\partial o}{\partial v}\cdot\frac{\partial v}{\partial w}$

lec05kp06-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp06-p4-34.text:
A negative gradient (the slope of the cost
with respect to one weight) means raising
that weight lowers the cost.

lec05kp06-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp06-p5-7.text:
Error signal δ: δ ≡ −∂E/∂v, the “error times slope”; it is passed
back along the weights.

lec05kp06-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp06-p6-35.text:
Backpropagation: after the forward pass, walk back from the output
layer; a hidden unit's δ is the sum of the next layer's δ times the

steps.label: Backprop slope
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp06 with view-from-text-v3: pages were planned first and each page is mainly one native infographic (designed in HTML and converted to native nodes), with the terms defined on the same page. 10 pages; every number is computed by program.

steps.label: Step has no slope
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP06. Prerequisites: the slope (derivative), for example the slope of y equal to x squared at x equal to 3 is 6; the partial derivative, moving one input while the others are fixed; and the chain rule. To let the network learn its weights we must look at the slope of the cost with respect to each weight and move in the direction that lowers the cost. The cost function adds up how far the prediction is from the target into one number, here E equal to one half of (t minus o) squared; gradient descent looks at the slope of the cost with respect to each weight and nudges the weight in the direction that lowers the cost. A step function has slope 0 everywhere except at the jump, where it has no slope, so gradient descent has nothing to use. The sigmoid has a tangent slope of 0.25 at x equal to 0. Next, the next page covers the sigmoid and the slope parameter a.

steps.label: Sigmoid and a
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the step having no slope. This page rounds the step into a sigmoid: f of x equals 1 over 1 plus e to the minus a x, and the slope f prime equals a times f times 1 minus f, so the slope can be computed from the function value itself. The sigmoid squeezes any number into 0 to 1, and the larger a is, the more the curve looks like a step. The figure uses a equal to 0.7, 2 and 8, and the slope peaks are a over 4: 0.175, 0.5 and 2 (computed by program). The common myth is that the closer to a step the better; in fact the larger a is, the narrower and higher the slope peak and the flatter both sides, so training by gradient gets harder. Away from the step the cube-vertex picture of KP03 no longer holds, and correct classification is carried by the cost function. Next, the next page covers the forward pass of the 2–2–1 network.

steps.label: Forward pass
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the sigmoid and the slope parameter a. This page runs the forward pass of a 2-2-1 network: 2 inputs, 2 hidden units and 1 output unit, each unit having 3 weights (a bias and two inputs). The input x is (1, 0), the target is 1, a is 1 and eta is 0.3. Hidden 1 is (minus 0.10, 0.20, 0.40), giving v1 of 0.10 and y1 of 0.525; hidden 2 is (0.10, minus 0.30, 0.20), giving v2 of minus 0.20 and y2 of 0.450; the output is (minus 0.20, 0.50, minus 0.40), giving vo of minus 0.118 and o of 0.471. The error e equals 1 minus 0.471, which is 0.529, and E equals one half of e squared, which is 0.140 (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the chain rule.

steps.label: Chain rule
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the forward pass of the 2–2–1 network. This page uses the chain rule to get the gradient of one weight. E depends on the weight w through o and v, so the partial of E with respect to w equals the partial of E with respect to o, times the partial of o with respect to v, times the partial of v with respect to w. Take the weight wo1 from hidden 1 to the output: the first is minus (t minus o), which is minus 0.529; the second is o times 1 minus o, which is 0.249; the third is y1, which is 0.525, the input this weight multiplies. The product minus 0.529 times 0.249 times 0.525 is minus 0.069 (computed by program). The gradient is negative, so raising wo1 lowers E. Next, the next page covers the error signal δ.

steps.label: Error signal δ
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the chain rule. This page combines the first two slopes. The sign convention: delta equals minus the partial of E with respect to v, the error times the slope; for the output unit delta-o equals e times f prime of vo, which is 0.529 times 0.249, equal to 0.1319. The gradient of E with respect to w equals minus delta times the input of this weight, for example minus 0.069 equals minus 0.1319 times 0.525; the descent direction adds eta times delta times the input. The inputs of the three output weights are 1, 0.525 and 0.450, eta is 0.3, and the updates are plus 0.0396, plus 0.0208 and plus 0.0178, all positive because the target 1 is above the output 0.471. The source writes delta both as the partial of E with respect to v and as error times slope, which differ by a sign; this lecture fixes delta as minus the partial of E with respect to v. Next, the next page covers the δ of the hidden layer.

steps.label: Hidden δ
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the error signal δ. This page is backpropagation: after the forward pass computes all outputs, walk back from the output layer. A hidden unit j affects E only through the weights to the next layer, so delta j equals f prime of vj times the sum over the next layer of delta k times the weight wkj. The index j numbers the hidden units, k the units of the next layer, here only the output unit; wo1 is 0.50 and wo2 is minus 0.40. Delta 1 equals 0.2494 times 0.1319 times 0.50, which is 0.0164; delta 2 equals 0.2475 times 0.1319 times minus 0.40, which is minus 0.0131; wo2 is negative, so delta 2 is below 0 (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the update of the nine weights.

steps.label: Nine updates
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the δ of the hidden layer. This page moves each of the nine weights one step, eta equal to 0.3. Each row is one weight: the gradient equals minus delta times input and the update equals eta times delta times input. The output bias goes from minus 0.2000 to minus 0.1604, the output w1 from 0.5000 to 0.5208 and the output w2 from minus 0.4000 to minus 0.3822; the bias and x1 weight of hidden 1 each gain 0.0049; those of hidden 2 each lose 0.0039; x2 is 0, so the two x2 weights do not move this time. A new forward pass gives output o moving from 0.4706 to 0.4857 and E falling from 0.1401 to 0.1322 (computed by program). One step is small, so many steps must be repeated. Next, the next page covers the numerical check.

steps.label: Numerical check
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the update of the nine weights. This page checks the gradients with numerical slopes. The central difference nudges one weight by plus or minus epsilon, equal to 10 to the minus 6, and divides E of w plus epsilon minus E of w minus epsilon by 2 epsilon. Over the nine weights, minus delta times input and the difference slope differ by at most about 3.8 times 10 to the minus 11 (recomputed by program with the same weights as the table and a equal to 1). The bars are minus delta times input and the dots are the difference slopes; they coincide, so the backpropagation formulas are right. This is the most common debugging method when writing a backpropagation program. Next, the next page covers slope saturation.

steps.label: Slope saturation
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the numerical check. This page looks at slope saturation. At x equal to 3, f prime of 3 equals a times f times 1 minus f: 0.068 for a equal to 0.7, 0.0049 for a equal to 2 and 3 times 10 to the minus 10 for a equal to 8 (computed by program), about 8 orders of magnitude below the value at a equal to 0.7. When a is too large the function saturates not far from the centre, delta is multiplied by an almost-zero slope and the weights barely move. So a is chosen at a middle size. Next, the next page covers the exercises.

steps.label: Exercises
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on slope saturation. Two exercises. Keep the example with a equal to 1 and eta equal to 0.3 but change the target from 1 to 0; the forward pass is unchanged. Q1: the error e equals 0 minus 0.471, which is minus 0.471, and the output delta equals minus 0.471 times 0.249, equal to minus 0.1173; check: the output 0.471 must fall toward 0, so delta should be negative. Q2: delta w equals 0.3 times minus 0.1173 times the input: bias minus 0.0352, w1 minus 0.0185, w2 minus 0.0158, all three move down; check: the signs are exactly opposite to the target-1 case (computed by program). That ends this unit; next, move on to the next unit.
